young.html: Aristotle said that human beings are political animals. He didn't mean we all love politics! He meant that we are made to live together in communities: families, villages and towns, where people share work, rules and friendships. Bees and ants live in groups too, but only humans can talk about what is fair and unfair, and make laws together.

Aristotle and his students collected the constitutions (the basic rules of government) of about 158 Greek cities, to compare them, a bit like a scientist collecting leaves. He noticed that a city can be ruled by one person, by a few people, or by many. Each kind has a good version, when rulers care about everyone, and a bad version, when rulers care only about themselves.

young.name: gb-constitutions
young.cap: Aristotle's six kinds of government. Tap a box to read about it.

young.html: Who decides? With your family, list some decisions: what's for dinner, where to go on vacation, bedtime, what game to play. For each one, who decides now: one person, a few, or everyone? Is that the best way for that decision? Why? Aristotle would say different questions may need different answers.
He thought a city works best when many of its people are neither very rich nor very poor, but in the middle, because they are steady and fair-minded and keep the other two groups from fighting.

full.html: The Politics, in eight books, comes from Aristotle's lectures in Athens (about 335–322 BC), where he taught at the Lyceum after years of studying and teaching elsewhere, including at the Macedonian court as tutor to the young Alexander. It follows the Ethics: having asked what a good life is, Aristotle now asks what kind of community makes it possible. The Great Books set adds The Athenian Constitution, a history of the government of Athens.

full.text: Book I: the city is natural

full.html: Families join into villages, and villages into a city (polis), which exists not just for life but for the good life. So the city is natural, and so is our need of it:

full.text: Hence it is evident that the state is a creation of nature, and that man is by nature a political animal.
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. X, Clarendon Press

full.text: But he who is unable to live in society, or who has no need because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god: he is no part of a state.
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. X, Clarendon Press

full.html: Only humans have speech, Aristotle says, which lets us share a sense of what is good and bad, just and unjust. Book I also discusses the household and money-making, which he thinks should serve the good life and not become an end in itself.

Slavery. In Book I, Aristotle defends slavery, claiming some people are slaves “by nature.” He notes that others in his own day said slavery was against nature and unjust. His view was used to defend slavery in later centuries, and it has been rejected: today it is universally condemned. We name it plainly here so readers know it is in the book.

full.text: Book II: other people's ideal cities

full.html: Aristotle reviews proposals for the best city, including Plato's. Against the Republic's sharing of property and families, he argues that a city made too unified stops being a city, and that what is common to the greatest number gets the least care. He also examines the constitutions of Sparta, Crete and Carthage.
A citizen, for Aristotle, is someone who shares in judging and ruling. He then sorts constitutions by who rules and for whose good:

full.name: gb-constitutions
full.cap: One, few or many, ruling for the common good or for their own good. Aristotle says the real line between oligarchy and democracy is wealth.

full.html: He considers the case for letting the many rule. Each may be ordinary, but together they may judge better:

full.text: For the many, of whom each individual is but an ordinary person, when they meet together may very likely be better than the few good, if regarded not individually but collectively, just as a feast to which many contribute is better than a dinner provided out of a single purse.
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. X, Clarendon Press

full.html: He also argues that the law, rather than any single person, should rule wherever it can, with rulers deciding only what the law cannot settle in advance.

full.text: Books IV–VI: real cities, the middle class and revolutions

full.html: Aristotle turns from the ideal to what works. Most cities, he says, would do best with a polity, a mixture of the rule of the few rich and the many poor, resting on a large middle class:

full.text: Thus it is manifest that the best political community is formed by citizens of the middle class, and that those states are likely to be well-administered, in which the middle class is large, and stronger if possible than both the other classes, or at any rate than either singly…
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. X, Clarendon Press

full.html: Book V studies why constitutions are overthrown: above all, quarrels over fairness, when one side thinks it is getting less than its due. Cities last, he says, when they guard against small changes, keep officials honest, and educate citizens in the spirit of their constitution.

full.text: Books VII–VIII: the best city and education

full.html: Aristotle sketches the best city he can hope for, with its size, land and citizens, and ends with education. Children should learn reading and writing, physical training, drawing and music, not only for use but for the right use of leisure, which he thinks is the aim of a good life.

This history of Athens' government, from its early kings through the reforms of Solon and Cleisthenes to the democracy of Aristotle's own day, was lost for centuries. A copy on papyrus from Egypt reached the British Museum and was published in 1891. It was probably written by Aristotle or one of his students, as part of the collection of 158 constitutions.

Reading Aristotle's “democracy” as the modern word. In his scheme it means rule by the poor many in their own interest, the bad twin of polity. His good form, polity, is closer to what many people today mean by a constitutional government. Words like this change meaning over time.

deep.html: The Politics was translated into Latin in the 1260s, and Thomas Aquinas, later on this ladder, wrote a commentary on it. Its idea of a mixed government, with power balanced among one, few and many, passed through Polybius and Cicero to later writers, among them Montesquieu and the authors of The Federalist (also on this ladder), who discussed checks and balances. Its picture of the human being as political, needing a community to live well, stands against the view of Hobbes and others that government is an agreement made by individuals out of fear.

Critics have rejected Aristotle's defense of slavery and his view that women should not share in ruling. Others still draw on his ideas of citizenship, the rule of law and the middle class. Readers disagree about how to weigh his insights against these views.

items: Are people naturally made for living together, or do they come together by agreement?
Can a crowd of ordinary people decide better than a few experts? When?
What does a good citizen do? Is a good citizen always a good person?

questions: Aristotle says we are “political animals” because we can talk about what is fair. What do you talk about with your family that is about fairness?
Who should make the decisions in a family, a team or a class? Does it depend on the decision?
Is a meal everyone brings food to better than a meal made by one cook? How is that like a group making a decision?
Aristotle was wrong about slavery. How can a very wise person be badly wrong about something important? What does that teach us about reading old books?
What makes rules fair? What happens when people think rules are unfair?
Why might it help a town if most people are neither very rich nor very poor?
care: Aristotle defends slavery in Book I and excludes women from ruling; the lesson names these plainly as views later thinkers rejected. Political ideas are presented with their critics, without modern political comparisons.
